Hong Kong Oil & Gas Producers Resume Operations After Week-Long Port Blockade Ends

HONG KONG, June 11—Oil and gas producers in Hong Kong have resumed normal operations following the lifting of a week-long maritime blockade that had disrupted shipments and halted exports from several key terminals, industry officials said Tuesday.

The blockade, which began on June 3, was imposed by an unnamed regional government in response to what it described as “unresolved disputes over commercial shipping rights and offshore resource access.” The measure targeted major oil and gas export terminals in Hong Kong’s Kwai Tsing and Tuen Mun districts, effectively preventing tankers from entering or leaving the ports.

The action left more than a dozen vessels stranded offshore, delaying the delivery of crude oil and liquefied natural gas cargoes and forcing some production facilities to scale back output. According to the Hong Kong Oil & Gas Producers Association, daily export volumes fell by 68 percent during the blockade, costing the sector an estimated HK$2.7 billion ($345 million) in lost revenue.

“After intense negotiations, we are relieved that the blockade has been lifted and our members are able to restore critical supply chains,” said Elaine Chu, spokesperson for the association. “We thank the Hong Kong special administrative region government and international mediators for their swift intervention.”

The dispute was resolved late Sunday following talks in Macau, industry and diplomatic sources said. Officials from the Hong Kong SAR, along with representatives from the affected oil and gas producers—including Southpoint Energy, Maritime Fuels, and Eastern Crescent Petroleum—reached a provisional agreement with the regional authority behind the blockade. Details of the accord have not been made public, but sources familiar with the matter said it includes commitments to resume dialogue on maritime boundaries and resource-sharing protocols.

“We welcome the outcome and are committed to ensuring the uninterrupted flow of energy resources from Hong Kong,” said Lin Wei, managing director of Southpoint Energy, in a statement. “Our crews are working around the clock to clear the backlog and resume scheduled deliveries.”

Analysts said the blockade highlighted the vulnerability of Hong Kong’s oil and gas producers to geopolitical tensions in the region. “Even a short disruption can have severe financial and operational consequences, given Hong Kong’s role as a critical export hub,” said Chen Liang, senior energy analyst at Pacific Rim Insights.

The Hong Kong Oil & Gas Workers Union said it was monitoring the situation closely as crews returned to work. “We are relieved no injuries occurred, and we urge all parties to prioritize stability for the sake of workers’ livelihoods,” said union chairperson Marco Lee.

Industry leaders said they expect operations to return to normal levels within the next few days.
